Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

a lot adverb

also lots, a lot of, lots of, very much, much, not much, much more, much better, greatly

classical

Catull. 50.2: multum lūsimus
Cic. Att. 8.13.2: multum mēcum mūnicipālēs hominēs loquuntur (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 85: multum temporis

multum

adverb; with a genitive, a lot of

a lot, much; often

With a verb, “a lot”; with a genitive, “a lot of”: multum temporis, a lot of time.

Other words

  • valdē — very much, really

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 1.1.5: valdē mē dēlectat

    Above all with verbs of liking.

  • 1magnopere: short final e (Lewis & Short magnŏpĕrē, marking it like an adverb in -ē). The ablative of opus, which ends in a short -e like every third-declension ablative: the phrase magnō opere written as one word, as the manuscripts of Terence and Cicero still divide it, and as maximō opere, majōre opere show (Lewis & Short, s.v.).

    magnopere1 (magnō opere) — greatly, very much; earnestly

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 15.14.4: ego tibi Rōmam properandum magnō opere cēnseō (Lewis & Short); Caes. BG 2.5: magnopere cohortātus (Lewis & Short)

    With verbs, above all of wishing, asking, urging and wondering: magnopere velle, ōrāre, mīrārī. With adjectives very rare (use valdē). Plautus, Caesar and Livy write it as one word; the best manuscripts of Terence and Cicero have magnō opere (Lewis & Short).

  • multus, multa, multum — much; in the plural, many, lots of

    adjective · also used · classical · Traupman 40: multum … tempus līberum habeō; Traupman 41: Multa.

    Multa on its own is “lots of things”.

  • plūrimum — very much indeed, most

    adverb · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 1.7.1: ut tē plūrimum dīligam (Lewis & Short)

  • multō (+ comparative) — much (with comparatives): much more, much better

    adverb (the ablative of the measure of difference) · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.48: quī multō plūs efferunt quam accēpērunt; Cic. Fam. 4.1.1: multō ante (Lewis & Short)

    With comparatives and with ante, post: multō plūs, much more; nōn multō post, not long after (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • hesternō, Licinī, diē ōtiōsī multum lūsimus in meīs tabellīs

    yesterday, Licinius, with time on our hands, we played a lot on my writing tabletsCatull. 50.1–2

  • vīlla mihi valdē placuit

    I liked the house a lotCic. Q. fr. 3.1.1

  • Multa. Pilā lūdō.

    Lots of things. I play ball.Traupman 41

  • an imitārī agrōs fertilēs, quī multō plūs efferunt quam accēpērunt?

    or to imitate fertile fields, which give back much more than they received?Cic. Off. 1.48

See also a little, cost a lot, that’s enough!, many, more, most, more.
